body:
The idea was that because it's a Listed element it should have the same general-purpose APIs as the other Listed elements: https://lists.whatwg.org/pipermail/whatwg-whatwg.org/2009-August/064766.html. I'm not sure how much sense this makes though.

I'm also not sure how much sense it would make for constraint validation to check `fieldset` elements. They are not form controls after all.

> I'm also not sure how much sense it would make for constraint validation to check fieldset elements. They are not form controls after all.

https://jsbin.com/nucekozegi/1/edit?html,output (see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6868 for motivation) is an example where I think it would make sense. I.e. saying "something in how you've input into this fieldset is invalid", when it might not be possible to pinpoint specific elements.

FWIW, we often have forms where one of two fields is required (e.g., first or last name, phone or email, etc.). Since a `<fieldset>` is the right semantics for grouping fields, it seems like it would be appropriate to set the custom validity at the fieldset level—and be able to use `myFieldset.validity` and `myFieldset.validationMessage` for displaying feedback to the user.

Fieldset supports `:invalid` and other Constraint Validation stuff, so it stands to reason a developer should be able to `setCustomValidity()`. 

Addresses are a good example where a _combination_ of address fields may satisfy the application's requirements. Independent validation of individual fields in this use case is not really helpful because their validity depends on what else has been done in other fields:
- address line 1 (required if line 2 is empty)
- address line 2 (required if line 1 is empty)
- city (required if zip code is empty)
- state (required if zip code is empty)
- zip code (required if city or state are empty)

The application could run that custom validation logic on submit and set an appropriate message based on what it finds using `fieldset.setCustomValidity(message)`, which triggers `:invalid` on the fieldset and other Constraint Validation features.

Another example would be date inputs. For credit card date expiry the `type="month"` input is not ideal since it doesn't reflect the format that is on the card.

A `fieldset` containing two textual inputs separated by a `/` makes an ideal input (static input masking is simpler to implement). But validating that a month is in the future implies parsing both dates and I don't want the validity popup to show for the inputs individually, I want it to popup on the `fieldset`.

Multistep forms, make use of this; aka: sequential step wizards, sequence forms, progressive disclosures, tabbed forms or tab list forms, and conditional forms etc.

Currently there's only so far you can get with HTML and CSS before javascript becomes a requirement when making multistep forms.

It's needed for multiple reasons

- forms are not nestable, _though fieldsets are_
- submit is all or nothing acting on an entire form, not form parts
- there's no HTML "validate" input type button to act on parts of form. example , your on Step # 1 of a two step form and only fields in fieldset # 1 need to validate on the frontend before revealing step#2
- a fieldset can't be set to work independently using HTML-only with it's own submit input(<input type="submit">) to trigger basic validation of it's child form-controls, instead submit inputs submit the entire form; even hidden invalid inputs.
- the [formaction](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/input/submit#formaction) attribute is on the input not the fieldset
-  [submit buttons don't participate in constraint validation; they have no real value to be constrained MDN input submit docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input/submit#formmethod:~:text=Submit%20buttons%20don%27t%20participate%20in%20constraint%20validation%3B%20they%20have%20no%20real%20value%20to%20be%20constrained.) ; _I've forgotten the example of why I had this bullet point but have it here for reference_ 
- HTML5 introduced the [form attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLInputElement/form) for form controls to aid seperated content that can't be in a heirarchy, however support is good only for *modern* browsers. Examples are page builders that such as ecommerce where the payment button and quantity are of the same form but in different parts of the UI in seperate hierarchies.
- Other elements like div or section do not recognize the disabled attribute for disabling form controls


So in multistep forms it's either:
- separate forms with servers - every step/page is a literal separate form with a roundtrip submission process to a backend if that's even an option available.
- a scattering of inputs all get related to a target form using the [form attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLInputElement/form) on each input ; **IF** you can determine the forms ID before or after rendering html that is.
  - or a javascript polyfill or javascript proxy to fill hidden inputs to a main form.
- grouping form-controls in _steps_  with containing elements using disabled and validation behaviors as conditions to trigger steps / allow the user to proceed ; even if only one input.

Grouping can be done with other elements but fieldset's disabled-attribute behavior helps prevent early use of a visible field(s) meant to be filled only at a specific phase.
Other elements like div or section do not recognize the disabled attribute for disabling form controls
